Before the middle of the fifteenth century, a book in Europe was made one copy at a time. A scribe, often in a monastery or a university town, wrote out every page by hand. A long text could take months. Errors crept in with each copy, and every copy was expensive enough that most people never owned one.

## What Gutenberg actually combined

Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith in Mainz, is credited with bringing several pieces together in the 1440s and 1450s rather than with inventing a single machine:

- **Movable metal type**, cast in a hand mould so that every letter of a kind came out the same size.
- **A metal alloy** of lead, tin and antimony that melted easily, cast cleanly and was hard enough to survive printing.
- **An oil-based ink** that stuck to metal, unlike the water-based inks used for woodblocks.
- **A screw press**, adapted from presses already used for wine and olive oil, to push paper evenly onto the inked type.

None of these parts was entirely new on its own. Movable type had existed in East Asia centuries earlier, first in ceramic and later in metal. What changed in Mainz was a system that made each extra copy cheap once the type was set.

## The Bible as a proof

The best known product of the workshop is the Bible printed in Mainz in the mid-1450s, often called the 42-line Bible after the number of lines in most of its columns. Estimates suggest that around 180 copies were made, some on paper and some on vellum, and a few dozen survive in libraries today. It was meant to look like a fine manuscript, and it did.

## Fixed cost, falling marginal cost

The economics are the interesting part. Setting a page of type took a lot of skilled work, but once it was set, printing another sheet took minutes. The cost moved from every copy to the first one. That changed what was worth producing: pamphlets, grammars, calendars, indulgences and, within a few decades, a large market for books across Europe.

> When copies become cheap, the scarce thing is no longer the copy but the attention of the reader.

The same pattern shows up in every later shift in how text is copied: the steam press, the photocopier, the web. Each lowered the cost of the next copy, and each moved the hard problems somewhere else, to editing, to trust, and to deciding what was worth reading.

## A lesson for anything that publishes

Cheap copying rewards care at the source. A printed error was repeated hundreds of times, so printers learned to proofread before a run. A website that rebuilds from source files on every change has the same property: whatever is checked before the build is right everywhere, and whatever is not is wrong everywhere.
